scholarly_argument_telfer_origin_of_aute.quote_verbatim: Yet an adjective αὐτεξούσιος is in evidence as far back as Chrysippus in the third century B.C. while, in due course, Adamantius, in the late third century A.D., presents us with παντεξούσιος as a divine predicate on the same pattern. […] The notion of autexousia is present with the classical philosophers, but not in such wise as to make them feel the need for a name for it. When the need came to be felt, it was met by the adjectival noun τὸ αὐτεξούσιον. But this does not appear until the second Christian century. Justin Martyr introduces us to the notion of autexousia as a universal human prerogative, using in this connexion the adjective αὐτεξούσιος.
scholarly_argument_telfer_origin_of_aute.context: Foundational philological claim of the article: the adjective αὐτεξούσιος is pre-Christian (Chrysippus 3rd c. BC, hostile/neutral/laudatory tones), but the substantive τὸ αὐτεξούσιον as a universal human prerogative is a 2nd-c. Christian neologism introduced by Justin Martyr. Telfer also notes the form αὐτεξουσιότης 'though in evidence only in the Christian era' (p.123). The arg is already e1-wired (pub_evidence_attached=true, 2026-05-19).

scholarly_argument_telfer_free_will_and_.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Justin and Jewish-Hellenistic origins, JTS p. 124)
scholarly_argument_telfer_free_will_and_.quote_verbatim: Thus the Christian doctrine of human autexousia, as it appears in Justin, has relations with Jewish angelology, and because of this was committed to a notion of parity, in respect to autexousia, between men and angels. Latin thought on liberum arbitrium started from human psychology, and was never committed in this way. So the march of Christian thought on the subject of human free will may be said to have stepped off with different feet in East and West.
scholarly_argument_telfer_free_will_and_.context: Programmatic thesis-statement of the article: Greek Christian autexousia and Latin liberum arbitrium have different conceptual origins — Hellenized-Jewish angelology vs. human psychology — hence the East/West divergence on free will from the 2nd century onward.

scholarly_argument_telfer_justin_martyr_.quote_verbatim: But even Justin's employment of αὐτεξούσιος in this connexion can hardly be original. There must have been known to him a whole field of apologetic literature belonging to Hellenized Judaism, now lost to us, from which he can have derived both vocabulary and ideas. This may indeed be gathered from a passage in the Second Apology. Here Justin, after showing that he thinks well of Stoic ethics, blames the determinism of Stoic science as cutting the ground from under every ethic.
scholarly_argument_telfer_justin_martyr_.context: Telfer's source-critical hypothesis: Justin did not coin τὸ αὐτεξούσιον ex nihilo but inherited it from lost Hellenized-Jewish apologetic literature. The Second Apology passage referenced is 2 Apol. 7 (anti-Stoic determinism + autexousia of γένεα).

scholarly_argument_telfer_christian_aute.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (parity of angels and men, JTS p. 124)
scholarly_argument_telfer_christian_aute.quote_verbatim: In this Second Apology, Justin says that God made the race of men and the race of angels alike self-determining (γένεα αὐτεξούσια), and looked forward to crowning their right use of this prerogative with the gift of incorruptibility. He does not, however, revoke the prerogative, even if used only to earn punishment. In the Dialogue, Justin, alluding to the philosophic commonplace of the ethical significance of praise and blame, claims that angels and men are only subject to either because they are αὐτεξούσιοι, and that they would not be so unless they were able to turn to the good or to the evil, indifferently (ἐπ᾽ ἀμφότερα τρέπεσθαι).
scholarly_argument_telfer_christian_aute.context: Direct textual evidence (Justin 2 Apol. + Dialogue with Trypho) for the parity-thesis: angels and humans share αὐτεξούσιον on identical terms, a feature absent in Latin liberum-arbitrium discourse. The Greek phrases γένεα αὐτεξούσια and ἐπ᾽ ἀμφότερα τρέπεσθαι are Telfer's own quotation from Justin (extracted as 'yevea avre£ovola' and 'eV dfjuf>6repa rpiireadaC' due to polytonic OCR loss).

scholarly_argument_telfer_east_west_dive.quote_verbatim: Thus the Christian doctrine of human autexousia, as it appears in Justin, has relations with Jewish angelology, and because of this was committed to a notion of parity, in respect to autexousia, between men and angels. Latin thought on liberum arbitrium started from human psychology, and was never committed in this way. So the march of Christian thought on the subject of human free will may be said to have stepped off with different feet in East and West.
scholarly_argument_telfer_east_west_dive.context: Same locus as scholarly_argument_telfer_free_will_and_determinism_in_e_0 — the two args paraphrase complementary halves of the same sentence-cluster (one focused on the angelological starting-point, the other on the East/West methodological divergence). Telfer's metaphor 'stepped off with different feet' is the canonical formulation cited in subsequent literature (e.g. Karamanolis 2013).

scholarly_argument_telfer_gnostic_reject.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Gnostic determinism and Clement's response, JTS pp. 124-125)
scholarly_argument_telfer_gnostic_reject.quote_verbatim: The more logical dualists of Alexandria rejected autexousia. According to Basilides and Valentinus, the Gnostic inclines to good by nature and embraces gnosis with the arms of faith, while the rest of mankind incline to evil by nature and are incapable of faith. This was the challenge which confronted Clement of Alexandria.
scholarly_argument_telfer_gnostic_reject.context: Telfer's framing of the Alexandrian dualist challenge: Basilides and Valentinus held a natural-class doctrine (πνευματικοί vs. ψυχικοί/ὑλικοί) that denied autexousia, and this is the polemical context for Clement's defence of universal moral self-determination in the Stromateis.

scholarly_argument_telfer_development_of.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (semantic evolution of αὐτεξούσιος; shift to τρεπτότης, JTS pp. 123 and 126)
scholarly_argument_telfer_development_of.quote_verbatim: Its earliest use is to describe a quality of certain subjects which differentiates them from many others. This quality is independence. Like 'independent', αὐτεξούσιος was susceptible to tones of a good, neutral, or disparaging kind. […] The notion of autexousia is present with the classical philosophers, but not in such wise as to make them feel the need for a name for it. When the need came to be felt, it was met by the adjectival noun τὸ αὐτεξούσιον. But this does not appear until the second Christian century. […] The assertion of human autexousia against fatalism was no longer so dominant a consideration, and attention was turning from autexousia itself to what we may call its shadow, τρεπτότης, considered as moral and spiritual precariousness.
scholarly_argument_telfer_development_of.context: Composite philological-historical claim assembled from p.123 (pre-Christian adjective with 3 tonal registers; abstract noun emerges only 2nd c. CE) and p.126 (4th-century shift of attention toward τρεπτότης and the process toward ἀτρεψία). Telfer's three-stage trajectory: independence-adjective → 2nd-c. abstract noun → 4th-c. correlation with moral precariousness.

scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_deter.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Church rejection of Origen's prenatal-sin scheme, JTS pp. 125-126)
scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_deter.quote_verbatim: Origen includes human autexousia among his First Principles. But his argument drives him back upon his theory of prenatal sin. It was consequently from the Christian tradition of angelology that he constructed his grandiose scheme of a redemptive world-process ending in the salvation of all creatures. The church, however, found the basis of this scheme out of harmony with scripture, and rejected emphatically Origen's theory of the prenatal fall of the soul. Thereafter Greek Christian teaching on human autexousia had to make a fresh start, assuming that the soul is innocent at birth and has before it the possibility of sinlessness, notwithstanding that the world, the flesh, and the devil may in fact render the possibility nugatory.
scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_deter.context: Footnote 4 to 'First Principles' refers to De Principiis 'iii. 1'. Telfer's claim: ecclesiastical rejection of Origenian prenatal-fall + apokatastasis forced a methodological restart for Greek anthropology, taking the soul as innocent at birth. This argument is the bridge between Origen and the 4th-c. consensus described later (pp. 126-127).

scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_syste.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Origen on autexousia as First Principle, JTS p. 125)
scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_syste.quote_verbatim: Origen includes human autexousia among his First Principles. But his argument drives him back upon his theory of prenatal sin. It was consequently from the Christian tradition of angelology that he constructed his grandiose scheme of a redemptive world-process ending in the salvation of all creatures.
scholarly_argument_telfer_origen_s_syste.context: Companion arg to telfer_origen_s_determinism_and_its_r_3, focused on the systematization side rather than its ecclesiastical reception. Telfer's footnote 4 specifies De Principiis iii. 1 — i.e. Περὶ αὐτεξουσίου, the third book's first chapter, which is precisely the text edited in Philocalia 21-27 (SC 226, Junod 1976).

scholarly_argument_telfer_grace_and_free.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Clement on grace and autexousia, JTS p. 125)
scholarly_argument_telfer_grace_and_free.quote_verbatim: In this process of moral thought Clement sees divine philanthropy wooing men to choose the good more powerfully than the demons, by exploiting inordinate passion, are able to coax them to evil. For God, as it were, feeds into the working process of moral autexousia impulses to repent, and on repentance divine Wisdom prompts faith, leading to election and salvation. Clement is not explicit as to the manner of divine grace, but his concern is so much with the conscious activity of mind as to make grace appear natural rather than mysterious.
scholarly_argument_telfer_grace_and_free.context: Telfer's characterisation of Clement's grace-doctrine: divine philanthropy operates by suasion into the natural functioning of autexousia (impulses to repentance → faith → election → salvation), making grace 'natural rather than mysterious'. The passage immediately follows Telfer's quotation of Strom. v. 13 and references to Strom. i. 17 and Paed. i. 6, i. 9 in the footnotes.

scholarly_argument_telfer_basil_the_grea.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Basil: autexousia as the image of God, JTS pp. 126-127)
scholarly_argument_telfer_basil_the_grea.quote_verbatim: In the optimism of that age, autexousia, in spite of its acknowledged possibilities of ill, came to be regarded chiefly as the prerequisite of the process of salvation by divinization. Basil the Great, therefore, calls autexousia 'the image of God', rather than the concomitant gift of reason. An image can be seen in something only potentially like, and in many ways unlike, its archetype, and autexousia makes man potentially like God. Nothing that had not autexousia could conceivably be or become like God, who is, in the phrase of Adamantius, παντεξούσιος. Thus autexousia formed the εἰκών whose hallowed use would end in ὁμοίωσις.
scholarly_argument_telfer_basil_the_grea.context: Footnote 3 to 'Basil the Great' refers to In ps. xlviii. 8 (Homilia in psalmum 48, §8). Telfer's claim: Basil locates the imago Dei in αὐτεξούσιον itself rather than in reason — a 4th-c. shift situating self-determination at the centre of the theology of divinization (εἰκών → ὁμοίωσις).

scholarly_argument_telfer_nemesius_of_em.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (Nemesius and the Antiochene anthropology, JTS pp. 127-128)
scholarly_argument_telfer_nemesius_of_em.quote_verbatim: The first formal work of Christian anthropology was by Nemesius of Emesa, whom Professor K. I. Duobouniotis called the master-exponent of the notion of autexousia as it occurs in Greek Orthodox doctrine. Nemesius discovers that the soul's autexousia is only exercised under manifold limitations arising from its union with the body. In practice it can only be exercised in situations which afford it an even possibility of doing this or that. The two sides of the even possibility are not simple situations but are immensely complex in structure. […] The delicate mechanism of the brain mediates a trio of faculties, sense, imagination, and memory, together under the presidency of reason. […] The Nemesian notion of conditioned moral decisions remains the crown of Greek thought on autexousia, but its synergist nature must be observed.
scholarly_argument_telfer_nemesius_of_em.context: The keystone passage for Telfer's reception-history thesis: the Antiochene synthesis culminating in Nemesius of Emesa (De natura hominis) is 'the crown of Greek thought on autexousia' — a synergist, body-conditioned account in which the soul exercises self-determination only under the joint mediation of the sensorium, the brain, and divine Providence. Directly relevant to Romain's thesis on the final transmission of the antique free-will debate through late-Greek patristics.

scholarly_argument_telfer_new_testament_.chapter: AUTEXOUSIA (scriptural grounding of autexousia, JTS p. 124)
scholarly_argument_telfer_new_testament_.quote_verbatim: Of course, the idea itself was not original with Justin. The notion of autexousia as a prerogative of all men is so abundantly present in scripture, and particularly in the New Testament, that it is an essential of Christian thought. But even Justin's employment of αὐτεξούσιος in this connexion can hardly be original.
scholarly_argument_telfer_new_testament_.context: Telfer's qualifying caveat to the philological argument: although the technical term τὸ αὐτεξούσιον is a 2nd-c. coinage, the underlying notion of universal human self-determination is biblically grounded ('abundantly present' in the NT). Telfer notes (implicitly) that Paul does not use the αὐτεξούσιος terminology — the arg-description's parenthesis 'though Paul does not use the term αὐτεξούσιος itself' is inferred from the article's silence on Pauline occurrences combined with the 'Justin introduces us to the notion' framing (p.123); it is not a verbatim claim by Telfer at this locus.

thesis_relevance_note: Telfer 1957 is directly load-bearing for Romain's thesis on the emergence of libertarian free will in early Christianity — specifically for (a) the philological-historical genealogy of τὸ αὐτεξούσιον from Chrysippus (adjective) to Justin Martyr (substantive); (b) the East/West divergence thesis (Greek autexousia vs. Latin liberum arbitrium starting points); (c) the reception of the antique debate through Origen → Antiochenes → Nemesius of Emesa as the 'crown of Greek thought on autexousia'. All 13 args are anchored in the same 7-page article via verbatim English quotation.
